discovery: Theory of quantum error correction and fault-tolerant, topologically protected quantum codes
subfield: Quantum information physics / quantum error correction
motivation: Quantum states were long considered too fragile to be preserved against decoherence, and the no-cloning theorem seemed to forbid redundancy. In 1995-1996 Shor and Steane independently discovered that quantum information can be encoded in entangled states of many physical systems so that errors can be detected and corrected without measuring the encoded information. Kitaev then showed that information can be stored in topologically ordered states of local lattice systems, the toric and surface codes, where errors are suppressed exponentially with system size below a threshold. These ideas revealed a new physical principle: quantum coherence can be actively stabilised indefinitely in noisy macroscopic systems. Over the past years, experiments with superconducting circuits, trapped ions and neutral atoms have implemented repeated stabiliser measurements and demonstrated logical error suppression as code distance grows, confirming this physics and making it the foundation of scalable quantum technologies.
